title: Potential stability and the balanced subcurve inequality
statement:
Let $g\geq2$ and $d>9(g-1)$ be integers, put $r=d+1-g$ and $P(m)=dm+1-g$. There is an integer $M(g,d)$, independent of the field, such that the following holds for every algebraically closed field $k$ [def-weil-field] and every $m\geq M(g,d)$. If a connected closed subscheme $C\subset\mathbf P^{r-1}_k$ with Hilbert polynomial $P$ has semistable $m$th Hilbert point for the linearization of [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization], then $C$ is a reduced curve of pure dimension one, all its singularities are ordinary nodes, and every genus-zero component of its normalization has at least two node branches. A node has completed local ring $k[[u,v]]/(uv)$. The hyperplane module $L=\mathcal O_C(1)$ embeds $C$ nondegenerately by its complete linear system, with $h^0(C,L)=r$ and $h^1(C,L)=0$. Let $\omega_C$ be the dualizing line of [lem-sfb-nodal-log-canonical-reconstruction] with no markings. For every nonempty proper reduced union $Y$ of irreducible components of $C$, let $k_Y$ be the number of nodes at which $Y$ meets the reduced union of the remaining components. Then
$$\left|\deg_Y L-\frac{d}{2g-2}\deg_Y\omega_C\right|\leq\frac{k_Y}{2}.$$
Here $\deg_Y$ is the sum of line-bundle degrees on the normalized components in $Y$ [def-pc-degree-line-bundle]. In particular, a smooth rational component meeting its complement in exactly two points has $\deg L=1$.

source.place: Section 3.2, Definition 7 and Theorem 8, printed pp.13--15, and equation (6) in Section 3.3. Local PDF WANTED; read online.

proof.text:
Put $h=g-1>0$, $r=d-h$ and $t=d/r$. Then $r>0$, $d\ge10$, and $1<t<9/8<8/7$. Use [lem-sfb-bounded-hilbert-weight-polynomials] with $B=4$, obtaining $A,m_0$. Increase $m_0$ to the uniform Hilbert-embedding bound of [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization]. Choose an integer $M\ge m_0$ with $M>2rA$. This depends only on $g,d$, since $P,r,B$ do. For any $m\ge M$ with semistable Hilbert point and any one of these weighted flags, the two inequalities in the weight lemma give
$$a_F\le t\sum_iw_i+\frac{A-h\sum_iw_i/r}{m}\le t\sum_iw_i+A/m.$$
The difference $a_F-t\sum_iw_i$ lies in $(2r)^{-1}\mathbf Z$. Since $A/m<1/(2r)$, it follows that $a_F\le t\sum_iw_i$. This conclusion holds simultaneously for all these flags on every curve in question. Denote it by (*).

source.place: Section 2.1 Proposition 1 and Lemma 2; uniformization for Section 3.2 Theorem 8

proof.text: The weight lemma gives $\dim C=1$. A field is Noetherian, and a projectively embedded scheme is finite type; [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-over-noetherian] therefore makes $C$ Noetherian. It has finitely many irreducible components by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components]. A zero-dimensional irreducible component would be a closed isolated point: it cannot meet another irreducible component without being contained in it. Connectedness and $\dim C=1$ rule this out. Thus $D=C_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a connected reduced curve of pure dimension one. The identification of coordinate Hilbert polynomial with Euler polynomial in [lem-sfb-flat-projective-hilbert-polynomial-locality], applied over $\operatorname{Spec}k$, gives $\chi(C,\mathcal O_C(n))=dn+1-g$ for every integer $n$.

source.place: Section 3.2, proof of Theorem 8, printed pp.14--15

proof.text:
Suppose a nonzero space $W$ of linear forms vanishes on $D$. Give it weight zero and its quotient weight one, so $s=\dim(k^r/W)<r$. The ideal of $D$ in $C$ is the nilradical. It is nilpotent: on a finite affine cover, finitely many nilpotent generators admit a common exponent, and the maximum of these finitely many exponents gives $N^q=0$. A nonzero restricted degree-$n$ monomial therefore has fewer than $q$ factors from $W$, so its weight is at least $n-q+1$. Thus
$$w_F(n)\ge(n-q+1)P(n),\qquad a_F\ge d.$$
But (*) gives $a_F\le ds/r<d$, a contradiction. Hence $D$ is nondegenerate. No bound on $q$ is needed: uniformity in $m$ already came from the bounded-weight lemma.

If the generic multiplicity along a reduced component of degree $e\ge1$ exceeded one, the component-projection lemma would give a zero/one flag with $s\le e+1$ and $a_F\ge2e+1/2$. Its hypotheses hold by steps 1--3. The inequality
$$2e+\tfrac12-\tfrac87(e+1)=\tfrac67e-\tfrac9{14}>0\quad(e\ge1)$$
contradicts (*) and $t<8/7$. Thus $C$ is generically reduced. If now a reduced component of degree $e\le3$ were not rational normal, the other projection estimate would give $s\le e$ and $a_F\ge e+1/2$. Since $e+1/2-(8/7)e=1/2-e/7\ge1/14>0$, this again contradicts (*). Consequently every such component is rational normal. These estimates concern component degrees on normalization, as specified in the cited lemma. Finally $\deg_C L=P(1)-P(0)=d$ in the Euler-degree convention. The component formula [lem-trf-degree-weighted-irreducible-components] now has all multiplicities one. Each component normalization is a smooth proper integral curve and is finite birational by [lem-trf-reduced-curve-normalization-genus]. The degree-one pullback formula [lem-sfb-proper-curve-bundle-pullback-degree] identifies its hyperplane degree with the component's Euler-degree. Consequently the sum of the normalized component degrees of $D$ is $d$, also before the finite-length nilradical is eliminated.

Apply the jet-weight lemma to $C$. Its generically reduced and nondegenerate hypotheses and its low-degree prerequisite were proved above. A ramified normalized branch would give $a_F\ge8$ with $\sum w_i\le7$, contradicting (*) and $7t<8$. A point of multiplicity at least three would give $a_F\ge3/2$ and $\sum w_i=1$, contradicting $t<8/7$. Finally a nonnodal double point, after all normalization maps are unramified, would give $a_F\ge7/2$ with $\sum w_i\le3$, contradicting $3t<24/7<7/2$. Thus every singularity of $D$ is an ordinary node, with the completed local ring in the statement. This includes double points with a tangent line component; their coefficient is $7/2$, so they cannot be discarded using only the larger coefficient for the other tangent case.

The hyperplane line on $D$ is very ample, since the reduced closed subscheme still embeds in projective space. If $H^1(D,L)$ were nonzero, [lem-sfb-nodal-special-clifford-subcurve] would supply a connected subcurve $Y$ with $e=\deg_Y L\ge2$ and $h^0(Y,L)\le e/2+1$. If $Y=D$, nondegeneracy gives $r\le h^0(D,L)\le d/2+1$, contrary to $r=d+1-g$ and $d>2g$. Suppose $Y$ is proper instead. It meets its complement, since $D$ is connected. Choose one such boundary branch on a normalized complementary component. Its hyperplane degree is a positive integer by [lem-trf-fibre-degree-ample-criterion], because it is the pullback of an ample line. For the selected single branch, the degree condition in [lem-sfb-subcurve-span-weight-bound] holds. That lemma and (*) yield
$$e+\tfrac12\le t\,h^0(Y,L)\le t(e/2+1).$$
But $e+1/2-(8/7)(e/2+1)=3e/7-9/14\ge3/14>0$ for $e\ge2$. This contradiction proves $H^1(D,L)=0$.

source.place: Section 3.2 proof step (7), Clifford support argument

proof.text: Let $N=\ker(\mathcal O_C\to\mathcal O_D)$. It is coherent, since $C$ is Noetherian, and its stalks vanish at every generic point by generic reducedness. Its closed support is therefore zero-dimensional, a finite set of closed points. By [lem-sfb-coherent-zero-dimensional-support], both $N\otimes\mathcal O_C(1)$ and $N$ have no higher cohomology, and zero global sections would force either to be zero. Tensor the reduction sequence by the invertible hyperplane line; this preserves exactness, as checked in any local trivialization. Cohomology across the closed immersion $D\to C$ is identified by [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-cohomology-edge]. The long exact sequence and step 6 give $H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(1))=0$. Vanishing in degrees at least two follows from [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension], since $\dim C=1$. Thus the Euler polynomial at $1$ gives $h^0(C,\mathcal O_C(1))=P(1)=r$.

source.place: Section 3.2 proof step (8), first half: finite support of the nilradical

proof.text:
The same long exact sequence now gives
$$h^0(D,L)=r-h^0(C,N\otimes\mathcal O_C(1)).$$
Nondegeneracy of $D$ means exactly that restriction of the $r$-dimensional space of ambient linear forms to $D$ is injective. Therefore $h^0(D,L)\ge r$, forcing $h^0(C,N\otimes\mathcal O_C(1))=0$. Global generation in [lem-sfb-coherent-zero-dimensional-support] gives $N\otimes\mathcal O_C(1)=0$, hence $N=0$ after tensoring with the inverse line. Thus $C=D$ is reduced, pure one-dimensional and nodal. Ambient linear forms inject into the $r$-dimensional $H^0(C,L)$ and so give an isomorphism. This proves completeness, nondegeneracy, $h^0=r$ and $h^1=0$.

source.place: Section 3.2 proof step (8), second half: eliminate embedded nilpotents by dimensions

proof.text:
For each nonempty proper reduced union $Y$ and its reduced complement $Z$, [lem-trf-nodal-subcurve-boundary] says that their intersection is precisely a finite reduced set of boundary nodes and that each has one smooth branch there on either side. Apply [lem-sfb-gieseker-component-interpolation] to the reduced complete nonspecial embedding obtained in step 8 and the inequalities (*) from step 1. For each normalized component $E$ of $Z$, its degree is at least the number $b_E$ of its boundary branches, or it is a rational normal component of degree $b_E-1$. In the latter case positivity of the hyperplane degree gives $b_E\ge2$. Thus all the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-subcurve-span-weight-bound] hold with every boundary branch chosen. It gives a zero/one flag with
$$\deg_YL+\tfrac{k_Y}{2}\le a_F\le t s\le t h^0(Y,L|_Y).$$
There is no connectedness requirement on $Y$ in that weight estimate.

source.place: Section 3.2 proof steps (9)--(10), full-boundary span flag

proof.text: For any such $Y$, let $K$ be the kernel of the surjection $L\to i_*(L|_Y)$ for its closed immersion $i:Y\to C$. This kernel is coherent, and [lem-sc-noetherian-cohomology-above-dimension] gives $H^2(C,K)=0$. The exact cohomology sequence and $H^1(C,L)=0$ then give $H^1(C,i_*L|_Y)=0$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-cohomology-edge] to $i$ to obtain $H^1(Y,L|_Y)=0$. Also $H^q(Y,L|_Y)=0$ for $q\ge2$ by the same dimension-vanishing statement. Hence $h^0(Y,L|_Y)=\chi(Y,L|_Y)$. This holds separately on each connected component if $Y$ is disconnected.

source.place: Section 3.2 proof step (10), nonspecial restrictions to subcurves

proof.text:
Apply [lem-trf-nodal-normalization-quotient] separately to each connected component of $Y$. Tensor its exact sequence by $L|_Y$. Local trivializations identify the resulting middle term with the finite direct image of the pulled-back line and the last term with one one-dimensional fibre per internal node. The quotient has the same Euler characteristic before and after twisting. Euler additivity [lem-pc-euler-additive] and the affine cohomology comparison for the finite normalization [lem-weil-pbc-affine-morphism-cohomology-edge] therefore give
$$\chi(Y,L|_Y)-\chi(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=\sum_{E\subset\widetilde Y}\bigl(\chi(E,L|_E)-\chi(E,\mathcal O_E)\bigr)=\deg_Y L.$$
The last equality is exactly [def-pc-degree-line-bundle] on each smooth normalized component. Combining with step 10 gives $h^0(Y,L|_Y)=\deg_YL+\chi(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$.

source.place: Section 3.2 step (10): normalization computation of subcurve Euler characteristic

proof.text:
Let $v_Y$ be the number of components of $Y$, $e_Y^{\mathrm{int}}$ its internal-node count (a self-node counts once), and $g_E$ the genera of its normalized components. Summing [lem-trf-nodal-curve-normalization-euler] over the connected components gives
$$\chi(Y,\mathcal O_Y)=v_Y-e_Y^{\mathrm{int}}-\sum_Eg_E.$$
The unmarked degree formula of [lem-sfb-nodal-log-canonical-reconstruction] gives, on the same components of the whole nodal curve $C$,
$$w_Y:=\deg_Y\omega_C=\sum_E(2g_E-2+\text{node branches on }E)
=-2\chi(Y,\mathcal O_Y)+k_Y.$$
Each internal node contributes two branches, each boundary node one. For $Y=C$, the same count and $\chi(C,\mathcal O_C)=P(0)=1-g$ give $w_C=2g-2$. The dualizing-line lemma applies over $\operatorname{Spec}k$ with no markings: projectivity, connectedness, reducedness, purity and nodality were proved, and a finite-type scheme over a field is finitely presented and flat over that field.

source.place: Section 3.3 equation (6); component degree and Euler normalization formulas

proof.text:
Write $l_Y=\deg_YL$ and $\chi_Y=\chi(Y,\mathcal O_Y)$. Substitute step 11 in step 9 and multiply by $r>0$:
$$r(l_Y+k_Y/2)\le d(l_Y+\chi_Y).$$
Since $d-r=g-1=h$ and $\chi_Y=(k_Y-w_Y)/2$ from step 12, this rearranges to
$$h l_Y\ge (d/2)w_Y-(h/2)k_Y,$$
so $l_Y-dw_Y/(2h)\ge-k_Y/2$. This is an exact inequality: the integral-gap argument in step 1 removed the finite-$m$ error before we used any subcurve.

source.place: Section 3.2 step (10) and Section 3.3 equation (6), lower bound

proof.text: The component-degree definition is additive on complementary unions, so $l_Z=d-l_Y$ and $w_Z=2g-2-w_Y$; the equality $l_C=d$ also follows by applying step 11's normalization computation to $C$ and using $P(1)-P(0)=d$. The same boundary nodes give $k_Z=k_Y$. Apply step 13 to $Z$ and substitute these three identities. This yields $l_Y-dw_Y/(2g-2)\le k_Y/2$. Together the two bounds are exactly the asserted absolute-value inequality, including when $Y$ or $Z$ is disconnected.

source.place: Section 3.3 equation (6), complementary subcurve upper bound

proof.text:
Consider an irreducible component whose normalization has genus zero, and let $b$ count all node branches on that normalization. Its positive integral hyperplane degree is $l\ge1$ by [lem-trf-fibre-degree-ample-criterion], and its dualizing degree is $-2+b$ by [lem-sfb-nodal-log-canonical-reconstruction]. If $C$ is irreducible, the Euler/branch computation of step 12 gives $b=2g\ge4$. If the component is proper and $b\le1$, it has no self-node and hence is smooth; its boundary count is $b$ (and connectedness in fact gives $b\ge1$). The balanced inequality on that component would then give
$$\left|l-\frac d{2g-2}(-2+b)\right|\le b/2,$$
which is impossible since $l\ge1$ and $-2+b\le-1$. Thus every genus-zero normalized component has at least two node branches. Finally for a smooth rational component meeting its complement in two points, there are no internal self-nodes, $b=k=2$, and the dualizing degree is zero. The inequality gives $|l|\le1$, and positivity gives $l=1$.

lean.statement: theorem gieseker_potential_stability (g d n : ℕ) (hg : 2 ≤ g) (hd : 9 * (g - 1) < d) (hn : n + 2 = d + 1 - g) : ∃ M : ℕ, ∀ (k : Type u) [Field k] [IsAlgClosed k] (C : Scheme.{u}) (f : C ⟶ Spec (.of k)) (i : C ⟶ ℙ(HilbertPlucker.Coordinates n; Spec (.of k))), IsClosedImmersion i → ConnectedSpace C → i ≫ (ℙ(HilbertPlucker.Coordinates n; Spec (.of k)) ↘ Spec (.of k)) = f → ∀ (P : NumericalHilbertPolynomial), P.1 = Polynomial.C (d : ℚ) * Polynomial.X + Polynomial.C (1 - (g : ℚ)) → ProjectiveHilbertPolynomial.IsCoordinatePolynomial k (n + 1) i P.1 → ∀ (D : HilbertPlucker.Hilbert k n P) (m : ℕ), M ≤ m → ∀ (E : HilbertPlucker.Presentation D m) (x : PGLLinearization.fieldTest k k ⟶ D.H), HilbertPointRepresents C i D x → x.left (IsLocalRing.closedPoint k) ∈ E.semistable → ∃ (_lfp : LocallyOfFinitePresentation f), Nonempty (@GiesekerPotentialStabilityConclusion k _ g d n C f _lfp i)
lean.note: The conclusion structure packages exactly the potential-stability clauses; the helper predicate identifies the given curve with the pullback of the recorded universal Hilbert ideal.
